stances.claim: When Art stepped down from the Supreme Court in December 2006 there was no sense of disappearance -- he did not retreat into silence, he did not retreat into comfort, he did not retreat at all. The robe came off, but the vocation did not.
stances.rhetorical_move: December-2006 anchor + triple-no-retreat anaphora + robe-off-vocation-on titular pivot

stances.claim: Retirement, for him, was not an ending but a repositioning -- a shift from judgment rendered behind closed doors to judgment articulated in the open forum of public discourse; he had spent more than a decade shaping jurisprudence through decisions, now he would shape civic conscience through words.

In February 2007 he began writing a weekly column for the Philippine Daily Inquirer titled 'With Due Respect' -- the title was not accidental; it reflected both tone and posture: firm but civil, critical but disciplined, grounded in law yet attentive to human consequence. He wrote not as a partisan, nor as a scold, but as a former Chief Justice who understood how easily institutions could be weakened -- and how slowly they were rebuilt.

stances.claim: Each Monday readers encountered a familiar voice -- measured, precise, occasionally stern, often pastoral; he wrote about governance, corruption, constitutional limits, judicial independence, moral leadership; he wrote as someone who had seen power from the inside and understood how thin its moral margins could be.

stances.claim: It did not take long for the column to find its audience -- law students dissected it, policymakers bristled at it, judges quietly admired its restraint, ordinary readers trusted it because it did not shout.

In time the columns were gathered into books -- 'With Due Respect', 'With Due Respect 2', 'With Due Respect 3' -- each volume a ledger of civic conscience, each page insisting that democracy survives not on passion alone, but on restraint. Even in retirement Art remained accountable -- to history, to faith, to the discipline of thought.

one_paragraph_summary: Art's post-Supreme-Court chapter, opening with the titular insistence that retirement in December 2006 brought 'no sense of disappearance' -- 'he did not retreat into silence, he did not retreat into comfort, he did not retreat at all. The robe came off, but the vocation did not.' Retirement is reframed as 'not an ending but a repositioning -- a shift from judgment rendered behind closed doors to judgment articulated in the open forum of public discourse.' Having 'spent more than a decade shaping jurisprudence through decisions,' he would now 'shape civic conscience through words.' In February 2007 he launched a weekly column for the Philippine Daily Inquirer titled 'With Due Respect' -- a title not accidental, reflecting tone and posture: 'firm but civil, critical but disciplined, grounded in law yet attentive to human consequence.' He wrote 'not as a partisan, nor as a scold, but as a former Chief Justice who understood how easily institutions could be weakened -- and how slowly they were rebuilt.' Each Monday readers encountered a 'measured, precise, occasionally stern, often pastoral' voice on governance, corruption, constitutional limits, judicial independence, and moral leadership -- 'someone who had seen power from the inside and understood how thin its moral margins could be.' The column quickly found its audiences: 'law students dissected it, policymakers bristled at it, judges quietly admired its restraint, ordinary readers trusted it because it did not shout.' The columns were eventually gathered into a three-volume series ('With Due Respect' / 'With Due Respect 2' / 'With Due Respect 3') -- 'each volume a ledger of civic conscience, each page insisting that democracy survives not on passion alone, but on restraint.' Even in retirement, 'Art remained accountable -- to history, to faith, to the discipline of thought.'
